title: Infrastructure Operational Playbook: GPU Fleet, Capacity, Networking, IaC, CI/CD
author: Lina Zhang
body:
Overview

This operational playbook consolidates Redwood Inference's recommended practices for managing the GPU fleet and capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC module usage, CI/CD pipelines, and runbooks used by oncall and infra engineers. The goal is to provide a single, actionable reference for day-2 operations, incident response, and planned capacity changes.

Scope

- GPU fleet and capacity planning for hosted and dedicated clusters.
- Cloud accounts, VPC networking patterns, and peering used across AWS and GCP.
- Terraform/IaC module design, versioning, and release process.
- CI/CD pipelines for infra modules, runtime images, and migration jobs.
- Runbooks and playbooks for typical operational tasks (scale up/down, node replacement, model rollout support).

Ownership and contacts

- Infra Platform (primary): infra-platform@redwood.com, Pager: #infra-oncall (Slack)
- GPU Fleet SRE (secondary): gpu-sre@redwood.com
- Network/Cloud Core: cloud-net@redwood.com
- IaC Module Owners: see module OWNERS file in repo (git://infra/modules)

SLOs and Operational Thresholds

- Per-region provisioned GPU utilization SLO: maintain <= 70% average util across 24h window during business hours (09:00-18:00 local).
- Queue time SLO for Dedicated jobs: median queue < 90s, p95 < 300s.
- Node health: replace nodes with >2 disk or GPU ECC errors in 24h.
- Provisioning lead time: terraform plan -> apply should complete within 15 minutes for incremental changes; larger pool changes may take 30-90 minutes depending on cloud capacity.

GPU Fleet Capacity Planning

1) Demand forecasting
- Weekly telemetry export (BigQuery) contains model-serving throughput, token/sec, concurrency by customer tier and region. Use forecast script (infra/tools/gpu_forecast.py) with 95% confidence window to produce weekly commit recommendations.
- Inputs: active routes, expected rollouts (product), historical QPS, expected sequence length distribution.

2) Capacity buffers and safety margins
- Target operational buffer: 20% spare capacity reserved for burst and failover during high-priority rollouts.
- Emergency reserve: 10% additional on-call-managed spare capacity kept unallocated for incidents (managed via a separate terraform gw-reserve module).

3) Scaling policies
- Automated scale-up: triggered when rolling average GPU util across cluster >75% for 10m and queue length grows >50% relative to baseline.
- Automated scale-down: only allowed during low-traffic windows (00:00-05:00 region local) and when util <40% for 60m.
- Manual scaling: runbook-guided steps below for planned capacity changes.

Cloud Accounts & Networking

Network layout (high-level)
- Per-region VPCs with shared egress, central NAT and egress firewall managed by cloud-net.
- Subnet segmentation: control-plane subnets (private), serving subnets (private, GPU-enabled), management subnets (bastion, ci runners).
- Inter-region peering via Transit Gateway (AWS) or Shared VPC (GCP) for cross-region KV cache replication.

Security and connectivity
- Use VPC endpoints for object storage and KMS.
- All GPU hosts require customer-label tagging (customer_id, workload_tier) and must be associated with an IAM role scoped to minimum privileges.
- Peering changes require change-review and a 48h communication window to dependent teams.

Terraform / IaC Modules

Module design guidelines
- Small, single-responsibility modules (compute_gpu, network_vpc, gw-reserve, autoscaler_policy).
- Each module must include: README, examples/, OWNERS, regression tests in /test (terratest or kitchen-terraform).
- Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Breaking changes must bump MAJOR and include a migration guide.

Module release process
1. Branch off main -> feature/xxx.
2. Add tests and examples.
3. Open PR with changelog entry and module bump if needed.
4. CI runs terratest; upon success reviewers (OWNERS) approve.
5. Merge triggers release pipeline that tags module and publishes to registry (internal terraform registry).

Version pinning and rollouts
- Environments must pin module versions in root-level terraform.tfvars to avoid implicit upgrades.
- For major module upgrades, use canary rollout: apply to dev -> staging -> 10% of prod regions -> full prod. Use rollout script infra/tools/rollout_tf_module.sh.

CI/CD and Build Pipelines

Repo layout and pipelines
- Repos: infra/modules (terraform modules), infra/cluster (cluster configs), infra/images (serving runtime images and GPU drivers).
- Pipeline types: unit tests (terratest/kitchen), lint (tflint, checkov), plan (terraform plan with diff), gated-apply (manual approval for prod applies).

Pipeline best practices
- All terraform changes must pass 'terraform plan' in CI with a plan artifact attached.
- Plan artifacts are stored in secure S3/GCS and linked in PRs for reviewers.
- Production applies require 2 reviewers + infra-platform approver + runbook approved if change impacts capacity/networking.

Sample CI status gates
- Lint: tflint, tfsec => pass.
- Tests: terratest => pass.
- Plan approval: required for any resource that changes autoscaling, IAM, VPC, or GPU quotas.

Runbooks: Common Procedures

A) Replace failing GPU node (oncall)
1. Identify node in telemetry (prometheus -> node-exporter alerts: gpu_ecc_errors > threshold).
2. Cordon node: kubectl cordon <node>.
3. Drain safe: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data.
4. Mark for replacement in terraform: update node_count in compute_gpu module (or trigger autoscaler).
5. Apply: terraform apply -target=module.compute_gpu -auto-approve (only from infra CI runner or approved bastion).
6. Verify: new node passes healthchecks, pod scheduling resumes, GPU tests in infra/images test suite pass.
7. Decommission old node and rotate keys if compromised.

B) Emergency capacity scale-up (pgp incident)
1. Pager triggers conference bridge.
2. Confirm impacted region and workload.
3. Increase reserved pool: terraform apply -var 'reserve_increase=+X' module.gw-reserve.
4. Update autoscaler policy to more aggressive thresholds if needed (reduce trigger from 75% to 70%).
5. Monitor: queue times, p95 latency, and token throughput.
6. After stabilization, revert autoscaler and decommission extra capacity per postmortem schedule.

C) Terraform drift remediation
1. Run nightly drift job (infra/tools/tf_drift_check.sh) that compares state to desired config.
2. For detected drift in non-sensitive modules: open PR with plan to reconcile.
3. For sensitive modules (network, IAM): escalate to module OWNERS and open a change request.

Observability and Telemetry

- Dashboards: per-region GPU utilization, node health, queue lengths, node boot time, image build status. Dashboards live in grafana/infra/gpu-fleet.
- Alerts: critical (pager) for node failure rate > 5% in 5m, queue p95 > 5x baseline for 10m, control-plane API error rate >1% p10.
- Logs: centralized via Loki/Stackdriver; correlate instance lifecycle events with provisioning logs in cloud operations.

Change and Release Checklist (must pass before prod apply)

1. Tests: terratest and image smoke tests passed.
2. Plan artifact attached in PR with reviewer signoff.
3. Runbook authored and linked to PR for capacity-impacting or network changes.
4. Communication: 48h notice to dependent teams for peering/VPC changes.
5. Backup: snapshot critical state (DB, state bucket) and verify recovery steps.

Appendix: Terraform examples and snippets

1) Example compute_gpu module usage\n
module "compute_gpu" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com:redwood/infra/modules.git//compute_gpu?ref=v1.4.2"
  region = "us-west-2"
  cluster_name = "serving-us-west-2"
  instance_type = "p4d.24xlarge"
  desired_gpu_count = 120
  labels = { env = "prod", tier = "dedicated" }
}

2) Example autoscaler policy (terraform HCL snippet)

resource "infra_autoscaler_policy" "default" {
  name = "gpu-serving-policy"
  scale_up_threshold = 0.75
  scale_down_threshold = 0.40
  cooldown = 300
}

Contacts, escalation, and postmortem

- Oncall escalation: primary -> secondary -> infra director. Use #infra-oncall and the PagerDuty schedule.
- Postmortem expectations: written within 72 hours, include timeline, root cause, corrective actions, and a follow-up ticket with owners and due dates.
